newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Khmer Rouge hardliners deny holding Briton.
newsitem.headline: Khmer Rouge hardliners deny holding Briton.

text.p: Cambodia's Khmer Rouge hardliners have denied holding a British mine clearance expert and his interpreter, who have been missing since late March.

Nominal Khmer Rouge leader Khieu Samphan, in a letter to King Norodom Sihanouk dated November 12 but only released by the palace on Monday, said he had checked thoroughly for news of Christopher Howes and his Cambodian colleague Houn Hourth.

Khieu Samphan, who is believed to be with hardliners loyal to Pol Pot in or near the guerrillas' northern stronghold of Anlong Veng, said the search found "that the National Army of Democratic Kampuchea (Khmer Rouge) was not involved in this case".

Sihanouk wrote to Khieu Samphan on November 2 asking him for information on the two staff members of the British-based Mines Advisory Group and help in securing their release. It was the second time the king had written to Khieu Samphan on the issue.
The two were seized by armed men in the northwest province of Siem Reap on March 26.
Conflicting reports of their whereabouts and captors emerged over the following weeks but the government finally said they had been moved to Anlong Veng.
Khmer Rouge defectors told reporters in the northwest town of Sisophon on October 20 that the two men were alive and said that Howes was helping the hardliners produce landmines.

The Khmer Rouge, which has been blamed for the deaths of more than one million people during its 1975-79 rule, has been fighting the government since it reneged on a 1991 peace pact and boycotted U.N.-run elections in 1993.
The Maoist group has kidnapped more than a dozen Westerners since the coalition government was formed in 1993 and killed at least seven of them.
A major split in the Khmer Rouge in August and defections of thousands of guerrillas to the government in the past month has raised hopes for a happy ending to the Howes kidnap case.
